clinicalPearls: Acquired clonal stem-cell disorder from a somatic PIGA gene mutation, leading to loss of GPI-anchored surface proteins (including CD55 and CD59) that normally protect red cells from complement attack.
Classic triad is intravascular hemolysis, marrow failure/cytopenias, and a marked thrombotic tendency, though most patients present with only one or two of these features.
Morning hemoglobinuria is a well-known feature but is actually seen in only a minority of patients; hemolysis is often chronic and low-grade rather than dramatically episodic.
Thrombosis is the leading cause of death and characteristically occurs at unusual sites — hepatic (Budd-Chiari), portal, mesenteric, cerebral (dural sinus), and dermal veins.
Consider PNH in any patient with unexplained hemolysis plus cytopenia, or with venous thrombosis at an atypical site, especially with a normal or low platelet count.
PNH clones frequently coexist with, precede, or follow aplastic anemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, reflecting a shared marrow-failure background.
Smooth muscle dystonia (esophageal spasm, erectile dysfunction, abdominal pain) results from free-hemoglobin-mediated nitric oxide scavenging rather than mechanical obstruction.
Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (e.g., FLAER, CD55/CD59) on granulocytes and red cells is the diagnostic test of choice, replacing older Ham's and sucrose lysis tests.
harrison.pathophysiology: PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a hematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor required to display several surface proteins. Loss of the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) leaves the abnormal red cell clone vulnerable to unchecked complement-mediated intravascular lysis. The clonal population expands, often in the setting of an immune-mediated marrow injury that gives PIGA-mutant cells a relative survival advantage, producing the combination of hemolysis, cytopenias, and a pro-thrombotic state linked to platelet and microparticle complement activation.
additionalDifferentials: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm or cold antibody type)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome
Hereditary spherocytosis or other membrane defects
G6PD deficiency and other hemolytic enzymopathies
nonInfectiousMimics: Aplastic anemia without a PNH clone
Budd-Chiari syndrome from other hypercoagulable states
additionalInvestigations: Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (FLAER, CD55, CD59) on granulocytes and erythrocytes — confirms and sizes the PNH clone
Complete blood count with reticulocyte count — documents hemolysis and identifies coexisting cytopenias
LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin — supports intravascular hemolysis
Urinalysis for hemoglobinuria and urinary hemosiderin — evidence of chronic intravascular hemolysis
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — should be negative, helping exclude autoimmune hemolysis
Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with cytogenetics — assesses for underlying aplastic anemia or MDS
Iron studies — chronic hemoglobinuria can cause iron deficiency despite hemolysis
Imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT/MR venography) if thrombosis at an atypical site is suspected
redFlags: Sudden abdominal pain, ascites, or hepatomegaly suggesting Budd-Chiari or mesenteric venous thrombosis
New neurologic deficit or severe headache raising concern for cerebral or dural venous sinus thrombosis
Rapidly worsening cytopenias suggesting evolution to aplastic anemia or MDS/leukemia
Severe abdominal or chest pain with hemolysis flare, which may signal smooth-muscle dystonia or thrombotic event
Pregnancy in a known PNH patient, which carries substantially increased maternal thrombotic and fetal risk
Acute kidney injury from massive hemoglobinuria or renal vein thrombosis
pitfalls: Assuming hemoglobinuria must be present and grossly visible; many patients have only subclinical or intermittent hemolysis
Missing the diagnosis in a patient with unexplained thrombosis at an atypical site because cytopenias are mild or absent
Relying on outdated Ham's/sucrose lysis tests instead of flow cytometry, which is far more sensitive and specific
Overlooking a coexisting or antecedent marrow failure syndrome (aplastic anemia, MDS) when a PNH clone is found
harrison.prognosis: Historically PNH carried significant mortality, largely from thrombosis and marrow failure, but complement-inhibitor therapy has markedly improved survival and quality of life. Long-term outcome also depends on clone size and any associated bone marrow failure syndrome, with a small risk of progression to MDS or acute leukemia over time.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Hemolytic Anemias and Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria
management: Control complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis with a terminal C5 inhibitor such as eculizumab or ravulizumab, or a proximal C3 inhibitor such as pegcetacoplan when residual anaemia persists
Vaccinate against meningococcus and other encapsulated organisms before starting complement inhibition, with antibiotic cover during the at-risk period
Treat thrombosis with anticoagulation and consider primary prophylaxis in high-risk patients with large clones
Provide supportive care with red cell transfusion, folic acid, and iron replacement as needed
Treat associated marrow failure with immunosuppression for aplastic anaemia, reserving allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation as the only curative option for severe marrow failure
Monitor haemolysis markers, clone size by flow cytometry, and for thrombotic events or evolution to myelodysplasia
